title: Costs and the bid-ask bounce
objectives: Account for costs and the bid-ask bounce.

screens.title: What a close price hides
screens.prose: A share's last trade of the day was a sale into the bid at £49.75. The quotes stand at £49.75 bid and £50.25 ask, so the mid is £50.00. A backtest buys at the close.
screens.question: What would a real buy order pay at that moment?

hints.text: Buy orders fill at the ask.

feedback.correct: Correct. A buyer pays the ask.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A buy order takes the best ask.

byKey.close: £49.75 is the bid, where the last trade printed. A buyer cannot buy there.
byKey.mid: The mid is a reference price. Nobody trades at it by crossing.

explain.text: The close printed at the bid, but a buyer pays £50.25, the ask. A backtest that buys at £49.75 gains half a per cent it could never have. Market microstructure's "Bids and asks" sets out the same book.

screens.title: Closes against mids
screens.prose: Pair (2, 3)'s spread through its trading period, on closes and on mids. Each close sits at the bid or the ask, half a per cent from the mid. Slide through the period.
screens.question: Which spread jumps more from one day to the next?

options.why: The mid spread is the smoother one: it has no bid-ask noise.
The average daily move is 0.0146 on closes against 0.0119 on mids.

hints.text: Each close adds ±0.5% of noise to its share.

feedback.correct: Correct. The bounce adds day-to-day noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at how jagged each line is.

byKey.mid: You picked the smoother line. Closes add the bid-ask noise.

explain.text: The average daily move of the spread is 0.0146 on closes and 0.0119 on mids. That extra noise is the **bid-ask bounce**: a close at the bid looks cheap, then bounces back. A same-day trade on closes buys that bounce.

screens.title: How much is bounce?
screens.prose: Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) worry that same-day returns include the bounce. Our full run gives the top 20's monthly committed return four ways.
screens.question: By how many percentage points does the same-day return on closes exceed the same-day return on mids?

feedback.correct: Correct. About 0.19 points a month is bounce.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the mids row from the closes row, both same day.

byKey.wait: That is the gap to the one-day wait, which also loses a day of convergence.

explain.text: Closes earn 1.00% and mids 0.82%, so about 0.19 points a month is bounce. The one-day wait gives 0.75%, a little below the mid run. It removes the bounce and also gives up one day of each move.

screens.title: Why waiting a day is conservative
screens.prose: The paper's wait-one-day rule opens and closes each trade a day after the signal, at that day's close.
screens.question: Why does this remove the bounce?

options.text: Tomorrow's close is at the bid or the ask independently of today's, so the trade no longer buys today's bounce

options.why: It still trades at a close; the close is simply a day later.
The wait does not add costs; it changes which price is used.

hints.text: Today's close may sit at the bid and make the share look cheap.
Tomorrow's close is a fresh draw, so no bounce is captured on average.

feedback.correct: Correct. A fresh close carries no stale bounce.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what links the signal's price to the fill's price.

byKey.mid: You assumed it trades at the mid. It uses the next close, which is a fresh draw.

explain.text: The signal fires on a close that may be at the bid. Filling at tomorrow's close, a fresh draw, breaks that link. It also gives up a day of convergence, so it is conservative.

screens.title: Four trades per round trip
screens.prose: Each round trip is four trades of £1: open long, open short, close long, close short. Charge a cost of $c$ per trade. Our top 20 make 1.69 round trips per pair per cycle with the wait.
screens.question: At c = 0.1%, what is the cost per pair per cycle?

hints.text: Four trades of £1 each round trip.

feedback.correct: Correct. About 0.68% per pair per cycle.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply 4c by the round trips.

byKey.once: You charged one trade per pair. Each round trip is four trades.
byKey.two: You charged two trades per trip. Opening and closing each leg makes four.

explain.text: 4 × 0.1% × 1.69 = 0.675% per pair per cycle. Against a gross 4.52% a cycle with the wait, that is a modest cut. The next screen finds the cost that wipes the profit out.

screens.title: The break-even cost
screens.prose: With the wait the top 20 earn 4.52% per pair per cycle, gross, from 1.6886 round trips.
screens.question: What cost per trade makes the net return zero?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the gross by four trades times the round trips.

byKey.perpair: You charged the cost once per pair. It is charged on every trade.
byKey.pertrip: You charged once per round trip. Each trip is four trades.

explain.text: c* = 0.0452 / (4 × 1.6886) = 0.00669, or 0.67% per £1 trade. The paper reports that profits survive conservative cost estimates. On our panel a cost below 0.67% a trade leaves a profit.

screens.title: Charging the cost once
screens.prose: A colleague subtracts a cost of $c$ once per pair per cycle and finds a break-even of 4.52%. They conclude the strategy survives any realistic cost.
screens.question: What is wrong?

options.text: Costs are paid on every trade: four per round trip and 1.69 trips, so break-even is 0.67%
Nothing: one cost per pair is standard
options.why: Every buy and every sell pays the spread and commission.

options.text: They should use the close as the fill price
options.why: The close may be the bid itself; that is the bounce, not a cost model.

hints.text: How many trades does one pair make in a cycle?
1.69 round trips, each of four trades.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each buy and each sell pays the cost.

byKey.right: You charged once per pair. A pair trades about 6.8 times a cycle, and each trade pays.

explain.text: Charged once, the cost looks harmless up to 4.52%. Charged per trade it breaks even at 0.67%, about a seventh as large. The cost count is as important as the cost level.

screens.title: A share with no bounce
screens.prose: Edge case. On mid prices there is no bounce at all. Waiting a day then costs only the day of convergence the trade gives up.
screens.question: On mids, how much does the one-day wait cost a month?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the mid wait row from the mid same-day row.

byKey.closes: That is the cost of waiting on closes, which also removes the bounce.

explain.text: On mids the wait costs 0.07 points a month, the day's lost convergence. On closes it costs 0.25, because it also removes the bounce. The two parts roughly add up to the close-price gap.

screens.title: Costs and the bounce in code
screens.prose: Write three functions. `bounce_effect` returns the three monthly committed means `(close_no_wait, close_wait, mid_no_wait)` with `step = 126`, using the loaded `run`. `net_of_costs` charges four trades per round trip. `breakeven_cost` solves for the zero-profit cost.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
def pairs_panel(seed=2006, n_ind=10, per_ind=10, n_pairs=20, days=3024, half_life=8.0, ou_sd=0.008,
                rw_sd=0.015, break_day=1512, break_frac=0.8, half_spread=0.005):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    N = n_ind * per_ind
    ind = np.repeat(np.arange(n_ind), per_ind)
    mkt = np.cumsum(0.0003 + 0.010 * rng.standard_normal(days))
    indf = np.cumsum(0.008 * rng.standard_normal((days, n_ind)), axis=0)
    phi = 0.5 ** (1.0 / half_life)
    u = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, N)), axis=0)        # unpaired: random walks
    common = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, n_pairs)), axis=0)
    eps = ou_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, 2 * n_pairs))
    a = np.zeros((days, 2 * n_pairs))
    for t in range(1, days):
        a[t] = phi * a[t - 1] + eps[t]                                   # mean-reverting gaps
    broken = rng.random(n_pairs) < break_frac
    drift = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, 2 * n_pairs)), axis=0)
    for k in range(n_pairs):
        for j in (2 * k, 2 * k + 1):
            x = common[:, k] + a[:, j]
            if broken[k]:                                                # the pair stops co-moving
                x = x + np.where(np.arange(days) >= break_day, drift[:, j] - drift[break_day, j], 0.0)
            u[:, j] = x
    pair_ind = np.repeat(np.arange(n_ind), 2)[:n_pairs]
    ind[:2 * n_pairs] = np.repeat(pair_ind, 2)                           # two planted pairs an industry
    logp = np.log(50.0) + mkt[:, None] + indf[:, ind] + u
    mid = np.exp(logp)
    bounce = np.where(rng.random((days, N)) < 0.5, 1 + half_spread, 1 - half_spread)
    close = mid * bounce                                                 # closes at bid or ask
    return close, mid, ind, broken


def normalise(P):
    P = np.asarray(P, dtype=float)
    return P / P[0]


def ssd_matrix(Pn):
    G = Pn.T @ Pn
    d = np.diag(G)
    return d[:, None] + d[None, :] - 2 * G


def top_pairs(Pn, k):
    D = ssd_matrix(Pn)
    i, j = np.triu_indices(D.shape[0], 1)
    order = np.argsort(D[i, j], kind="stable")[:k]
    return [(int(i[o]), int(j[o])) for o in order]


def trade_pair(form, trade, i, j, wait=0, open_at=2.0):
    sd = float(np.std(form[:, i] - form[:, j]))
    a, b = trade[:, i].tolist(), trade[:, j].tolist()
    n = len(a)
    payoff, opened, t = 0.0, False, 0
    while t < n:
        s = a[t] - b[t]
        if sd > 0 and abs(s) > open_at * sd and t + wait < n - 1:
            side = 1 if s > 0 else -1          # +1: i is dearer, so short i and buy j
            to = t + wait
            tc = next((u for u in range(t + 1, n) if (a[u] - b[u]) * side <= 0), None)
            tx = n - 1 if tc is None else min(tc + wait, n - 1)
            ri = (a[tx] - a[to]) / a[to]
            rj = (b[tx] - b[to]) / b[to]
            payoff += side * (rj - ri)
            opened = True
            t = tx + 1
            continue
        t += 1
    return payoff, opened

close, mid, ind, broken = pairs_panel()


def cycle_return(close, start, k, wait=0):
    Pn = normalise(close[start:start + 378])
    form, trade = Pn[:252], Pn[252:]
    res = [trade_pair(form, trade, i, j, wait) for i, j in top_pairs(form, k)]
    total = sum(p for p, _ in res)
    n = sum(1 for _, o in res if o)
    return total / k, (total / n if n else 0.0), n


def run(close, k, wait=0, step=21):
    return [cycle_return(close, s, k, wait)[0] for s in range(0, close.shape[0] - 378 + 1, step)]

screens.title: A desk's cost stack
screens.prose: A pairs desk pays 0.02% commission and half the bid-ask spread, 0.10%, on each trade. The short leg also pays a borrow fee of about 0.5% a year.
screens.question: Which of these does the paper's wait-one-day rule address?

options.text: The half-spread, through the bid-ask bounce in the close prices

options.why: The wait does not change what a broker charges.
The fee depends on how long the short is held, not on the fill price.
It removes only the bounce, a spread effect. The other two need their own charges.

hints.text: Only which close each trade fills at.
That targets the half-spread hidden in closes.

feedback.correct: Correct. The wait removes the bounce, a spread effect.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The wait changes the fill price, nothing else.

byKey.all: You assumed one rule covers every cost. Commission and borrowing must be charged separately.

explain.text: The wait removes the spurious bounce gain, which is a spread effect. Commission and the borrow fee remain and must be charged. On our panel the break-even is about 0.67% per trade, so a 0.12% stack leaves room.

ideas: Closes sit at the bid or the ask. A same-day trade on closes books a bounce nobody could capture.
Waiting a day fills at a fresh close, which removes the bounce and gives up a day of convergence.
Each round trip is four trades; break-even cost = gross / (4 × trips), about 0.67% here.
